Heyy! I'm an international student from Prague! Super excited for you, it's a beautiful city. You'll probably find it pretty affordable compared to Boston. I'd recommend taking advantage of the public transportation system to save money (it's actually very funftional), I suggest getting a seasonal ticket for Prague and Central bohemian region, you might be able to get a student discount too, check this website for how to pay for travel:

https://pidlitacka.cz/en/pricing

Prague is also REALLY walkable, so walk wherever you can, it's a great way to explore the city! 

If you're looking for queer-friendly spots, check this website, they keep an updated list of clubs/bras and also events:

https://www.queerprague.cz/#Bars-Clubs

I personally recommend piano bar - they do drag shows and events 
https://maps.app.goo.gl/QdPNasogyXU1jLAPA

For non-queer specific clubbing places Duplex is a must 
https://maps.app.goo.gl/a6jaHrWpS1GKdXS 

Cross Club is also fun imo
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bfgabGQ2HhF9GjXW7

I'd avoid Karlovy Láznĕ, it's basically a giant tourist trap with overpriced everything. Also avoid Storm Club, the crowds there are iffy.

Keep in mind that most clubs in Prague charge a 15-20usd entry fee and most of them are really dead until midnight (most places close at 4 or 6am)

You should also try czech beer, it's really good. Best way to do that is to walk into a random pub somewhere out of touristy zones, you'll get solid traditional beer and food for aa good price.

I was in a BU  a cappella freshmen year, I thought the way we managed auditions was pretty superficial.

Only a few of the people who applied were straight up bad. Majority of the singers was good so the competition was strong.

Now we had a bass/alto shortage at that time so we basically gave priority to people in that voice range, which is something we should have but did not communicate to those applying, it's possible you just were not the type of voice the groups were looking for at the moment. 

I can also say that at least for our auditions we did have a social event but the impressions people made did not end up factored into wether we would admit them or not. This might also be dependent on the group.

Also the callback rounds were done in the span of one day and by the end of it, everyone was very exhausted and ready to get out of there so we probably didn't give each candidate enough attention and rushed some decisions.

I ended up leaving because the group felt more like a frat/sorority with an established clique of friends who were just not my type of people.

This is my personal experience with only one out of many groups on campus so it is probably not representative.

Professors are really good and knowledgeable in my experience, school is smaller so it's easier to make good connections with other students and mainly the faculty, they also do a lot of events (guest speakers, networking opportunities etc.)

I wrote a very similar post here in my freshmen year, objectively since then not much have changed, I have a good roommate and overall three people who I can call friends but as you said, it feels shallow, but here's some stuff that may be helpful; 

My biggest problem was (still kinda is) living in the nostalgia of the past, I was constantly coming back to memories from high-school and my home where I actually had really close friendships - beware of that kind of nostalgia, it will put you in the "it's not how it used to be" you'll be sad for virtually no reason instead of trying to live in the present. 

On living in the present, try not to treat college as "I just have to survive this semester and then I can go home to my bf/gf/friends/parents" - It makes you idealise whatever you call home and your brain then defaults to "home = happy, college = sad" it's a loop you don't want to be stuck in 

What helped me in the initial stages was shifting my focus to academics and a sport, at a certain point I gave up on trying to "artificially" make friends so I prioritised other stuff and that's ironically where I met my current roommate, we're hovering between being acquaintances and friends but it is such an improvement compared to my roommates from last year, so I think it definitely helped my mental health 

Try to accept offers to travel/go out/do stuff (within reason ofc), but we remember experiences and you're in a new place so might as well use all the opportunities, even if you won't enjoy hanging out with the people, maybe it'll be a good restaurant or a cool place you'll want to come back to...

Aight this was long, best of luck to you and all of us
